title: Queue with Vec
story: The print shop has jobs piling up. First come, first served — the oldest job gets printed first, new jobs go to the back of the line. This is a queue: add to the back, remove from the front. Let's build one with a Vec!
why: Queues model any first-in-first-out system — task schedulers, message brokers, customer service lines, and printer spoolers — and building one manually teaches you fundamental data structure design.
analogy: A queue is like the line at a food truck — the first person to arrive gets served first. New arrivals go to the back. No cutting in line! Vec stores the people, enqueue adds to the back, dequeue serves the front.
try_it: Add a `Queue.peek[T](self) -> Option[T]` method that returns the front item without removing it. Then build a `process_queue` function that dequeues all items and prints them until the queue is empty. Simulate a real print shop: enqueue 5 jobs, then process them in a while loop. What happens when you dequeue from an empty queue?
tips: Enqueue = push to end. Dequeue = remove from beginning (rebuild without item 0). Simple in concept, verbose in code
Always check for empty: dequeue on an empty queue returns None — handle it gracefully
The rebuild pattern (new Vec, copy items except first, replace original) is the manual way to 'shift' a Vec
common_mistakes: Trying to 'remove' item 0 by reassigning — `self.items[0] = ...` doesn't shorten the Vec; you need a rebuild
Forgetting to clear the original Vec after building the new one — the old items remain and cause duplicates
Using pop() for dequeue — pop() removes from the END (LIFO, like a stack), not the front (FIFO)
